entry.title: DKIM "no key for signature" after switching to a 2048-bit key: the TXT record is probably cut off
entry.summary:
You generated a new DKIM key, published the TXT record, and the receiver says one of these: dkim=fail (no key for signature) dkim=permerror (bad key) dkim=neutral (key not found / DNS lookup failure)
Before blaming the mail server, look at what DNS is actually serving. A 2048-bit public key in base64 is around 390 characters, plus v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=. A single DNS TXT string can hold at most 255 bytes, so a longer value has to be published as several quoted strings in one record. Resolvers join them back together with no separator. Some DNS editors split the value for you, some do not, and some silently truncate at 255 characters. A truncated key still looks like a perfectly normal record, which is why this takes people hours. dig +short TXT selector1._domainkey.example.com

entry.title: From JSON to Markdown: Reducing AI SEO Analysis Token Costs by 90%
entry.summary:
AI SEO analysis pipelines usually run into two problems quickly. First, the more data you analyze, the more input tokens you send to the model. Adding more keywords, markets, competitors, pages, or result rows makes every prompt longer. That may not matter for a one-off analysis, but it matters when a pipeline runs thousands of times a day.
Second, cutting the input down can make the analysis less useful. When the full dataset does not fit into the model context, you might often split it into batches, summarize each batch, or rely on agent memory. Those techniques help, but they can not replace the original data. If positions 1-10 and positions 21-30 land in different batches, the model may never compare them side by side.

entry.title: Paste Messy Text into Excel as a Real Table, Using ChatGPT as the Parser
entry.summary:
Trip expenses often arrive as a few sentences in an email: who went where, when, and how much it cost. Paste that into Excel and the whole thing lands in cell A1. Splitting it by hand means retyping every value. TL;DR: Ask ChatGPT to turn the text into a table with the columns you name, copy the answer, and paste it into A1. Each value gets its own cell. Paste the text into ChatGPT and add one line (translated): Put the content below into a table. Columns, in order: name, department, destination, departure date, expenses (KRW).
Press Enter and use the copy button under the answer. Click A1 in Excel and paste. Name through expenses go into separate columns, and the expense values arrive as numbers, so you can calculate with them right away. ChatGPT sometimes adds a total row on its own. That row is a typed number, not a formula. If someone later corrects one expense, the total will be wrong and nothing will warn you. Click the total cell and press Alt+=. Excel inserts a SUM over the column above, and from then on the total follows any edit. In my test, four people's trip notes became a five-column table in about four seconds. The total was 497,000 KRW before and after switching to the Alt+= formula. Listing the columns fixes both the headers and their order. That matters when the table has to sit under last month's rows: the new data lines up without rearranging anything. Written with AI assistance. The steps were tested by hand before publishing.
